newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia debt futures fully prepared for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Australia debt futures fully prepared for rate cut.

text.p: FUTURES CASH YIELD
*Australian debt futures burst ahead after second quarter wages data came in weaker than expectations, fuelling already strong expectations of a monetary policy easing.
*10-year bond futures match all time peak of 93.630 on data.
Australian debt futures burst ahead after second quarter wages data came in weaker than expectations, fuelling already strong expectations of a 50 basis point reduction in official interest rates.
The September 10-year bond futures contract matched its all time peak of 93.630 set in early 1994, but there was some reluctance to enter uncharted territory before the rate move.
September bill futures hit 94.98 on the data, equating to a cash rate of 5.02 percent compared with official 5.5 percent interest rates.
Analysts said an easing could come as early as Friday.

Average weekly ordinary time earnings rose just 0.5 percent in the three months to May for an annual growth rate of 3.7 percent, an outcome that was even lower than the most optimistic of economists' forecasts.
The quarterly rise was the smallest since November 1993 and annual growth was at its lowest since August 1994. The annual rate is also well below the RBA's 4.5 percent comfort zone.

The data follows Wednesday's benign inflation data which showed the policy sensitive annual underlying rate at its lowest level since the series began in 1971 at 1.7 percent, and below the central bank's 2.0-3.0 percent target.

Bruce Hockman, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said that while a rate cut was possible on Friday, he would not be surprised if they waited until after the August 5 Reserve Bank board meeting.

"One of the issues they may want to consider at the Reserve Bank board meeting is should they move 50 basis points or should they do something greater given the softness in the economy...and the very good inflation outlook over the short to medium term," Hockman said.
He said the risk would be the market looking for a further 50 basis points in the not too distant future.
However, David de Garis at ANZ Banking Group did not think that a 50 or 75 basis point easing would convince the market either way that that's the end of the easing cycle.
"You could argue that 75 (basis points) might suggest a new phase of monetary policy to stimulate the economy even more and a signal of more to come," de Garis said.
The market's rally saw the Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread compress and test 25 basis points, its lowest level since the early 1980s.

U.S. Treasuries stayed around their New York price lows in early Tokyo trade, having given up some ground after Tuesday's heady rally amid profit-taking. Canadian debt underperformed the U.S. as it absorbed the supply of a C$1.3 billion 30-year bond auction.
